blocks.md: In a growing economy almost everything keeps rising — output, the capital stock, wages — so there is no fixed resting point in the raw numbers. A balanced growth path is the growing-economy version of a resting point: every variable grows at its own steady, constant pace, so the ratios between them stay put. The way to find it is to measure everything relative to what is growing — for example output per effective worker, which stays constant while the totals climb.

blocks.title: Why it matters
blocks.md: It is how growth models line up with the data, and it shows which growth rates are permanent and which are only temporary.

Growing economies have no steady state in levels. The trick is to **stationarize**: divide every variable by whatever is growing, find the steady state of the normalized system, then read growth rates back out. A balanced growth path is that normalized steady state, seen in levels.
With labor $L$ growing at $\eta$ and labor-augmenting technology $\tilde{A}$ growing at $\tilde{\gamma}$:

| Variable type | Notation | Example | Growth rate on the BGP |
| --- | --- | --- | --- |
| Per effective worker | $\tilde{x} = X/(\tilde{A}L)$ | $\tilde{k}$, $\tilde{y}$, $\tilde{c}$ | 0 |
| Per worker | $x = X/L = \tilde{x}\tilde{A}$ | $k$, $y$, $c$ | $\tilde{\gamma}$ |
| Aggregate | $X = \tilde{x}\tilde{A}L$ | $K$, $Y$, $C$ | $\tilde{\gamma} + \eta$ |
The growth rates follow from "the growth rate of a product is the sum of growth rates" ([Logarithms and Growth Rates](note:logarithms-and-growth-rates)).

Plotted on a log scale, each variable on a BGP is a straight line whose slope is its growth rate. Off the BGP (during transitional dynamics), per-worker growth is above $\tilde{\gamma}$ if the economy is below its steady state and below $\tilde{\gamma}$ if above.
Because $k = \tilde{k}\tilde{A}$ and $K = \tilde{k}\tilde{A}L$, logs turn products into sums:

Draw each piece against time and add them: $\ln\tilde{k}$ is flat on the balanced growth path, $\ln\tilde{A}$ is a line with slope $\tilde{\gamma}$, $\ln L$ a line with slope $\eta$. Any shock is then read off as a change in the pieces.

blocks.alt: Log growth paths - rise in population growth, capital per worker
blocks.caption: Hand-drawn: after a rise in population growth, $\ln\tilde{k}$ falls to a lower level; adding $\ln\tilde{A}$ (unchanged slope) gives a per-worker path that grows more slowly for a while and then runs parallel to, but below, the old path.

blocks.src: assets/Attachments/Log growth paths - rise in population growth, aggregate capital.png
blocks.alt: Log growth paths - rise in population growth, aggregate capital
blocks.caption: Adding $\ln L$, whose slope rises from $\eta_1$ to $\eta_2$, makes aggregate capital eventually grow faster, at $\tilde{\gamma} + \eta_2$.

blocks.md:
| Effect | What changes | Example |
| --- | --- | --- |
| **Level effect** | Per-worker path shifts up or down, same long-run slope | $s$, $\delta$, $\eta$, a one-off loss of capital |
| **Growth effect** | Per-worker long-run slope changes | $\gamma$ (technology growth) |
$\gamma = 2\%$ TFP growth with $\alpha = 1/3$ gives $\tilde{\gamma} = 0.02/(2/3) = 3\%$ labor-augmenting growth. With $\eta = 1\%$: output per worker grows 3%, aggregate output 4%.

Long-run growth in living standards (per-worker output) comes **only** from technology in the [Solow Model with Technological Progress](note:solow-model-with-technological-progress); saving and population affect levels, not long-run growth rates.
